title: Modular Inverses
short: a has an inverse mod n exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1; find it with the extended Euclidean algorithm.
trouble: Students expect every nonzero number to have an inverse, but 2 has no inverse mod 6 because gcd(2, 6) = 2: the multiples of 2 mod 6 are only 0, 2 and 4.

blocks.html: In ordinary arithmetic, dividing by $a$ means multiplying by $1/a$. Mod $n$ there are no fractions, but sometimes there is a number that does the same job. Finding it uses Bézout's identity, and knowing when it exists fixes the trouble with cancelling we met in modular arithmetic.
Definition. An inverse of $a$ mod $n$ is an integer $x$ with $ax \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$. We write $x \equiv a^{-1} \pmod{n}$.
Theorem. $a$ has an inverse mod $n$ exactly when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, and then the inverse is unique mod $n$.

$ax \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ means $ax - 1 = ny$ for some integer $y$, that is, $ax - ny = 1$. If $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, Bézout gives such $x$ and $y$, so an inverse exists. If $d = \gcd(a, n) > 1$, then $d$ divides $ax - ny$, which would mean $d \mid 1$: impossible. Uniqueness: if $ax \equiv 1$ and $ax' \equiv 1$, then $x \equiv x(ax') = (ax)x' \equiv x' \pmod{n}$.

blocks.name: nt-clock

opts.task: Mod 6, nothing lands on 1 when $a = 2$. Change $a$ to $5$. Now which point is sent to 1?

blocks.cap: Arrows from $x$ to $2x \bmod 6$ reach only 0, 2 and 4, so no $x$ has $2x \equiv 1$: 2 has no inverse mod 6. With $a = 5$ every point is hit once, and $5 \cdot 5 = 25 \equiv 1$.

blocks.title: Larger modulus: extended Euclid
steps: $101 = 17 \cdot 5 + 16$ and $17 = 16 \cdot 1 + 1$. The gcd is 1, so an inverse exists.
Mod 101 the multiple of 101 vanishes: $6 \cdot 17 \equiv 1$. Check: $102 = 101 + 1$.

head: $a$
blocks.cap: Every nonzero residue mod the prime 11 has an inverse. They come in pairs (2 and 6, 3 and 4, 5 and 9, 7 and 8), and only 1 and 10 are their own inverses, a fact that returns in Wilson's theorem.

blocks.html: Expecting every nonzero number to have an inverse. Mod 6 the multiples of 2 are only $0, 2, 4$, so $2x \equiv 1$ has no solution: $\gcd(2, 6) = 2$. Before hunting for an inverse, check $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Mod a prime $p$ the problem disappears: every $a$ with $p \nmid a$ has an inverse.
The numbers from 1 to $n$ that are coprime to $n$, and so have inverses, are called the units mod $n$. Counting them gives Euler's phi function.
$a^{-1} \bmod n$ exists exactly when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Find it with the extended Euclidean algorithm: from $ax + ny = 1$, the inverse is $x \bmod n$.
